title: Tool Authorization
why: Users need granular control over when tool executions require confirmation. The LLM currently executes all tools blindly, which can lead to unintended file modifications or destructive commands.
outcomes: Users can choose between auto-execute, ask-on-write, or ask-for-all modes. The LLM must declare destructive intent on bash calls. Pending tool calls are cancelled when the user adds instructions mid-execution.

milestones.name: Authorization Setting
milestones.objective: Add a user-configurable setting that determines which tools require confirmation before execution.
milestones.success: Settings exposes an Authorization field with three valid values. Invalid values fall back to auto.
milestones.diagram: Settings.json → Authorization field → parsed at startup → drives authorization gate behavior per tool call

tasks.name: Add Authorization field to Settings
tasks.what: Add Authorization string field to Settings struct in internal/config/settings.go with default value "auto".
tasks.why: Stores the user's preference for tool authorization mode: auto, ask-on-write, or ask-for-all.
acceptance: Settings struct compiles, defaults to "auto", rejects unknown values by falling back to auto

tasks.name: Add Authorization enum constants
tasks.what: Add AuthorizationAuto, AuthorizationAskOnWrite, AuthorizationAskForAll string constants in settings.go.
tasks.why: Avoid magic strings scattered across the codebase. Single source of truth for mode names.
acceptance: Constants match the three valid values, used in ValidateAuthorization

milestones.name: Destructive Bash
milestones.objective: Add a required destructive boolean field to the bash tool schema so the LLM must declare whether a command modifies disk state.
milestones.success: Bash tool schema requires destructive field, returns error if omitted. Tool tracks destructiveness on the result.
milestones.diagram: LLM → bash({"command": "rm -rf ...", "destructive": true}) → schema validates required field → Execute checks destructiveness → ToolResult carries Destructive flag

tasks.name: Add destructive to bash schema
tasks.what: Add destructive (boolean, required) to the bash tool JSON schema in internal/tools/bash.go.
tasks.why: The LLM must explicitly declare whether a bash command modifies files or system state. No default — omitting it returns an error.
acceptance: Schema is valid JSON, destructive is required, omitting it causes a validation error

tasks.name: Add Destructive field to ToolResult
tasks.what: Add Destructive bool to ToolResult struct in internal/tools/tools.go. Set it from args["destructive"] in the bash Execute function.
tasks.why: The authorization gate needs to know at execution time whether a tool is destructive, before running it.
acceptance: Destructive field populated on bash results, error returned when omitted

tasks.name: Mark inherently destructive tools
tasks.what: Add IsDestructive func()bool to the Tool struct. Set it true for write_file, edit_file, skill_build. Bash uses the runtime destructive arg.
tasks.why: The authorization gate needs a pre-execution way to determine if a tool is destructive, without running it first. For file tools, destructiveness is static. For bash, it comes from the args.
acceptance: write_file, edit_file, skill_build always report destructive. bash reports based on args. read_file, skill_load, skill_list, set_working_dir, open report false

milestones.name: Authorization Gate
milestones.objective: Intercept tool execution in the stream loop. When authorization mode requires it, pause and ask the user before executing. On rejection, cancel pending tool calls.
milestones.success: In ask-on-write mode, destructive tools pause for confirmation, read-only tools auto-execute. In ask-for-all, every tool pauses. Rejected or instruction-annotated tools cancel remaining pending calls and resume stream.
milestones.diagram: Stream → tool_calls stop → iterate partialTools → check authorization needed? → yes: enter ModeAuthorize → user responds (y/n + optional instructions) → execute tool or reject → if instructions injected: cancel remaining tools, resume stream immediately. else: continue to next tool

tasks.name: Add authorization types and constants
tasks.what: Create internal/app/authorization.go with AuthorizationResult enum (Accepted, Rejected, AcceptedWithInstructions) and AuthorizationContext struct holding the pending tool, args, user instructions, and result.
tasks.why: Encapsulates the authorization state machine: what tool is pending, what the user responded, and whether extra instructions were provided.
acceptance: Struct and types compile, provides all fields needed by the UI and execution logic

tasks.name: Add authorization mode to streamState
tasks.what: Add authorizationContext field to streamState in stream.go. Add pendingToolIndex int to track which partialTool is being authorized. Add needsAuthorization helper method on Model.
tasks.why: The stream loop needs to know when it's paused waiting for user authorization and which tool is pending.
acceptance: needsAuthorization returns true for all tools in ask-for-all, only destructive in ask-on-write, nothing in auto

tasks.name: Refactor executeTools to support authorization interruption
tasks.what: Rewrite executeTools in stream.go to check authorization before each tool execution. If authorization is needed, return a single AuthorizationContext and the caller (handleStreamEvent) pauses the stream. Remaining tools are left unexecuted until the user responds.
tasks.why: Currently executeTools runs all tools in a batch. With authorization, we must process one at a time and potentially pause for user input, canceling remaining tools on rejection or instruction injection.
acceptance: When no authorization is needed, behavior is identical to before. When authorization is needed, returns nil and sets authorizationCtx

tasks.name: Handle authorization response in stream event loop
tasks.what: In handleStreamEvent, after executeTools returns nil (authorization needed), transition to ModeAuthorize. After user responds: if Accepted → execute that single tool, check next tool. If Rejected or WithInstructions → mark remaining tools as cancelled, build entries with appropriate error/result, resume stream. If instructions attached → inject synthetic user message before resuming.
tasks.why: This is the core state transition: stream pauses → user decides → stream resumes with modified context.
acceptance: Accepted tools execute, rejected tools return error, instructions trigger synthetic message injection, remaining tools are cancelled

tasks.name: Inject synthetic user message on instruction-attached authorization
tasks.what: When authorization resolves with instructions, append a synthetic user message to the session containing the user's instructions, then resume streaming via startStream().
tasks.why: Breaks the assistant turn with user context, allowing the LLM to adjust its behavior before continuing.
acceptance: User message appears in session, stream resumes with the new message in context

milestones.name: Authorization UI
milestones.objective: Build the authorization prompt that appears in the status bar area: yes/no selection with arrow keys, tab to switch to instruction input, shift+tab to return to yes/no, enter to submit.
milestones.success: The authorization overlay renders in the status line area. User can navigate between yes/no, switch to text input, and submit. All keybindings work correctly and transition back to streaming or chat mode.
milestones.diagram: ModeAuthorize → render overlay (status line): [←] Yes / No [→] ←→ arrows, tab for text, enter to submit → user key event → if text mode: textarea input → if yes/no mode: arrow selection → enter: resolve authorization → resume stream or chat

tasks.name: Add ModeAuthorize to modes
tasks.what: Add ModeAuthorize to the Mode enum in internal/app/modes.go and its String() method.
tasks.why: Needed for the routing in Update/View to handle the authorization overlay as a distinct mode.

tasks.name: Build authorization prompt component
tasks.what: Create internal/ui/authorization.go with an AuthorizationPrompt struct that renders the yes/no prompt in the status bar area. Tracks selection (yes=0, no=1) and text mode (false=yes/no, true=text input).
tasks.why: Encapsulates the authorization UI: the prompt line showing tool name + args, the yes/no selection, and the text input for instructions.
acceptance: Component renders correctly, shows tool name, yes/no selection, and instruction hint

tasks.name: Add authorization prompt field to Model
tasks.what: Add authPrompt ui.AuthorizationPrompt to the Model struct in app.go. Populate it from authorizationCtx when entering ModeAuthorize.
tasks.why: The Model needs to hold the authorization prompt state so it can render and handle input.
acceptance: authPrompt is populated from authorizationCtx, setAuthMode initializes it

tasks.name: Render authorization overlay in View
tasks.what: In render.go View(), add a case for ModeAuthorize that renders authPrompt instead of the textarea, replacing the status line area.
tasks.why: The authorization prompt replaces the input area during authorization, making it the primary interaction point.
acceptance: In ModeAuthorize, the authorization prompt replaces the textarea in the layout

tasks.name: Handle authorization key input
tasks.what: Add handleAuthorizeKey to input.go: Left/Right arrows toggle Yes/No, Tab switches to text mode, Shift+Tab returns to yes/no, Enter submits. In text mode: normal text input, Enter submits with text, Shift+Tab returns to yes/no.
tasks.why: Routes authorization key events to the correct action: selecting yes/no, switching to text, or submitting.
acceptance: Left/Right toggles selection, Tab enters text mode, Shift+Tab exits text mode, Enter resolves. Text input works in text mode.

tasks.name: Wire authorization mode in Update dispatch
tasks.what: In update.go handleKey, add case for ModeAuthorize → handleAuthorizeKey. In handleStreamEvent, when executeTools returns nil, transition to ModeAuthorize.
tasks.why: Wires the authorization mode into the main event loop so it can intercept and respond to key events.
acceptance: Authorization mode is dispatched in handleKey, key events reach handleAuthorizeKey

milestones.name: System Prompt Update
milestones.objective: Update the system prompt so the LLM knows it must set the destructive field on every bash call, and understands the semantics of what makes a command destructive.
milestones.success: System prompt clearly defines destructive vs read-only bash commands. LLM consistently sets the correct value.
milestones.diagram: sys-prompt.go → DefaultAssistantPrompt() includes new bash destructive field instructions → injected into every API request as system message

tasks.name: Update system prompt for destructive field
tasks.what: Add a new section to the default system prompt in internal/config/sys-prompt.go explaining the destructive field for bash: when to set true, when to set false, and that the field is required.
tasks.why: The LLM needs explicit instructions to populate the required destructive field correctly on every bash call.
snippet:
## Bash Tool
- The bash tool requires a "destructive" boolean parameter on every call.
- Set destructive: true if the command modifies files, deletes data, creates directories, installs packages, or changes system state (e.g., rm, mv, cp, mkdir, chmod, apt-get, pip install, git commit, sed -i).
- Set destructive: false for read-only commands (e.g., cat, ls, grep, find, git status, git diff, wc, head, tail, df, ps, curl GET).
- Omitting the destructive field will result in an error.
acceptance: System prompt contains clear destructive field instructions for bash, examples of true and false cases

milestones.name: Resolve Authorization Response
milestones.objective: After the user responds to an authorization prompt, execute or reject the tool, handle remaining pending calls, and route back to either continued tool authorization or stream resume.
milestones.success: resolveAuthorization handles all four result types (Accepted, Rejected, AcceptedWithInstructions, RejectedWithInstructions). Pending tools are cancelled when instructions are injected. Stream resumes correctly with or without injected user message.
milestones.diagram: handleAuthorizeKey Enter → resolveAuthorization(result, instructions) → if Accepted: execute tool → check next partial (needs auth? → ModeAuthorize again / no → continue) → if WithInstructions: cancel remaining, inject user msg, startStream → if Rejected: mark rejected, cancel remaining, resume stream

tasks.name: Implement resolveAuthorization
tasks.what: Add resolveAuthorization method to Model in stream.go. Handles the four auth results: execute+continue for Accepted, mark error for Rejected, execute+cancel+inject for AcceptedWithInstructions, mark error+cancel+inject for RejectedWithInstructions.
tasks.why: This is the core post-authorization logic that determines what happens after the user responds — the branching point between continuing, cancelling, and injecting context.
acceptance: All four auth results are handled correctly. Single tool executes on accept, error on reject. Remaining tools cancelled on instructions. Stream resumes or user message injected.

tasks.name: Implement executeSingleTool and continueAfterAuth
tasks.what: Add executeSingleTool (extracted from old executeTools batch logic, for one partial) and continueAfterAuth (saves the assistant message with all entries, injects user message if needed, and either resumes stream or checks next tool for authorization).
tasks.why: Factored from executeTools so a single tool can be executed outside the batch, and the post-authorization flow can decide whether to resume streaming or continue checking more tools.
acceptance: Single tool execution mirrors batch behavior. continueAfterAuth saves message, handles injection, and resumes stream. Remaining tools are checked for authorization.
